falsifiable_question: Can a chartered investigator, with one falsifiable question and an allowed source class, test whether Medicare Advantage membership shrinkage is the mechanism of the margin change?
sampling_limitations: Desk research only. No interviews, surveys, or site visits. Three UnitedHealth filings only: the 2025 Form 10-K, the June 30, 2026 Form 10-Q, and the July 16, 2026 earnings release filed as an 8-K exhibit. CMS monthly Medicare Advantage enrollment files, separate plan or county exit notices, provider-network statements, competitor filings, and already-published customer reviews were not retrieved. usage.tool_calls counts five external retrieval calls, two web searches and three EDGAR filing-index fetches, and does not count local reads of the task packet or of text already retrieved. usage.sources counts the three cited filings. retrieval_timestamp is the UTC time the retrieved filing text was locked in this session, not an HTTP Date header. The company does not print a Medicare Advantage-only operating margin. The 965,000 figure and the Medicare Advantage row are different populations. No Q3 2026 document is in this source set. The three filings are the same filer and are not independent of one another.

findings: The 2025 operating-margin break is not explained by Medicare Advantage membership shrinkage. Consolidated operating margin fell from 8.1 in 2024 to 4.2 in 2025 and the medical care ratio rose from 85.5% to 89.1%, while the Medicare Advantage people-served row rose from 7,845 thousand to 8,445 thousand. UnitedHealthcare operating margin fell from 5.2% to 2.7%, and Optum Health operating margin fell from 7.4 to (0.3). Management names Medicare funding reductions, elevated medical cost trend, the profile of newly added value-based patients, decreased favorable development, the Inflation Reduction Act, and individual-exchange morbidity. It names growth in Medicare Advantage membership as a reason medical cost dollars rose.

The contraction comes later. The 2025 10-K expects 2026 Medicare Advantage membership to contract because of benefit and pricing actions taken under funding pressure. The June 30, 2026 10-Q prints 7,565 thousand versus 8,350 thousand a year earlier. The July 16, 2026 earnings release prints 7,565 thousand at June 30, 2026 versus 8,445 thousand at December 31, 2025. Over the year-earlier quarter, consolidated operating margin rose from 4.6% to 7.1% and the medical care ratio fell from 89.4% to 86.7%. Shrinkage coincides with the later margin repair, not with the 2025 break.

Counter-evidence to the tested mechanism is the 2025 direction of membership. Membership moved up while the margin broke, and the filed explanation of that break does not cite shrinkage. The investigation stopped on COUNTER_EVIDENCE_FOUND before using the remaining source budget.

What remains partial is the 2026 ratio. The June 30, 2026 10-Q attributes the medical care ratio decline to reserve development, affordability and medical cost management, and pricing, and does not name membership shrinkage. The July 16, 2026 earnings release attributes that same ratio decline to benefit design and pricing discipline, member mix, and medical cost management, and separately prints $860 million of net reserve development. Member mix is consistent with a smaller book, but neither document isolates how many points of the ratio came from Medicare Advantage shrinkage versus pricing, reserves, or cost management. The 10-Q does say medical cost dollars fell primarily because fewer people were served. That is a volume statement, not a ratio mechanism.

The 965,000 figure is a different population from the Medicare Advantage row. The earnings release applies 965,000 to seniors served through Medicare Advantage including complex populations included in Medicaid. The Medicare Advantage row in the same release moves from 8,445 thousand at December 31, 2025 to 7,565 thousand at June 30, 2026. The row agrees with the 10-K year-end figure and with the 10-Q comparison of 7,565 thousand versus 8,350 thousand.
Commercial risk-based membership did shrink in 2025, from 8,845 thousand to 8,165 thousand. That is not the Medicare Advantage row the question asks about.

Hypothesis impact, with no recommendation and no valuation. This role does not change H1-H5 plausibility. Those hypotheses remain Director-drafted and are not Founder-approved. The evidence is material to the mechanism they would use. H1 cannot treat the 2025 margin break as the result of Medicare Advantage membership loss, because that book grew. H2 is not shown to be permanent damage, but the filings describe multi-year Medicare funding pressure and a 2026 contraction caused by benefit and pricing actions. H3 is the hypothesis the evidence touches most directly: the 2025 margin damage occurred on a larger Medicare Advantage book, and the 2026 margin repair occurred on a smaller one, so the repair is not a same-book recovery and the economics are mixed. H4 is not tested. H5 is not tested, because no price work was done.

Unknowns left inside the stop: no CMS contract-level enrollment file, no county-exit notice beyond the filings' statement that the company chooses counties annually, no provider-network statement, no competitor filing, and no customer review. No Medicare Advantage-only margin bridge. No Q3 2026 document.
